films.descriptionHtml: I can see Sandra Wollner as a new, singular voice in world cinema. I binged her films today and found a consistent dread all over them. And everytime (pun intended) the dread manage to gives way to this mystical sense of hope in the end.

films.title: Paper Tiger
films.descriptionHtml: The rating might be partly biased, but Gray is increasingly becoming my favorite American filmmaker—I've loved most of his films, and I do think he is the last true master of the neoclassicists. Just like most of his last few entries (I haven't watched his early work yet; I'll get to that later, I promise), everything here is a question of mise-en-scène: the blocking, the camera movements, and where the characters move within the frame. It is so assured that we take it for granted, which is the highest compliment one can pay a director working in this tradition. Suspense and drama are also in good balance and feed each other, with the tension building from within each character rather than relying on editing tricks. And I would argue it’s the ending where the film transcends, making this his finest work to date—at least it feels like he has kept refining his methods over his last few releases, rather than this being an overall comment on his entire oeuvre, which I can't make for the reason mentioned above.

films.title: Look Back
films.descriptionHtml: Easily Kore-eda most mainstream move, openly pushing the sentimentality. With a source material as strong as this, it's obviously going to work whether you agree with his approach; like how he stretched a spans of their friendship and kindred love of art and shared labour to passing seasons and the toned-down nature of the character rivarly. But I do love it. The film feels good, and for the better of it, it lacks the hurried pace of the animated adaptation: it's a one-shot adaptation anyway, but my point is Kore-eda lets his scene breaths through the season changes. It is his usual cinema, though more firm in controlling our emotions, he uses a cue, scoring to guide when and what to feel, and that never felt overstated or a little too much. Those feel good nature also come from how much lived-in affection he builds up, the gesture, seasonal changes; winter expressed by the beautiful snowy Akita, or when cicadas sound humming in the background with a spinning fan in the summer. Nothing particularly big nor dramatic happened almost for the entire runtime, so when the tone shifts it does so quietly. I do think quiet devastates more than announced.

films.title: La Bola Negra
films.descriptionHtml:
the melodrama really swells here, and it's also gorgeous, it just lets the feeling be bigger than the scene. they really get this part right. loved me myself some maximalist movies.

but then, my quarrel is with some of the war shoot. The dead are composed like still life, couldnt stop debating over myself whether this is an ethic of the image or just an aesthetic of alibi? what it cost to make the intolerable vieweable (or consumable). here the answer seems to be that the cost is the intolerable itself. looks like beauty lauders the horror. it trying to have both an authority as historical witness, and yet also wanting the pleasure of tableau and refuses to choose which weights more.

the timelines also run in parallel yet never truly contamined one another. which i dont really have problem with, but it does made me wonder what couldve been if they treated this one like Sound of Falling, with the visual consistency across generation.

so yeah. undeniably it's very well made, well shot, well acted, but it's a lot. the ambition is huge, and as spectacle it lands just fine. what i'm less sure about is the creative judgement. i don't think it quite gets some of its choices right.

films.title: Tell Everyone
films.descriptionHtml:
oh my. i did not see this coming, and i liked it more than the melodrama i just watched, which is a sentence i'm still a little surprised to be typing, lol.

the thing is it offers so little, but it just executed flawlessly. there are no experiments with narrative flow, no gambling on formal choices, the screenplay is very straight and somehow that's probably the point? there's a kind of rigor in refusing to perform. the film trusts the scene and it's character, and doesn't reach past what it needs.

what i keep circling back to tho is the gaze. it's inoffensive in the best sense, i mean ethically inoffensive: it never once turns exploitative, not even when it has to look at a tragedy. there's a whole old argument about where the camera goes being a moral question, and here you just won't really find any problem with the shots. except, there's one shot maybe. Where i did wonder about the intention, whether it was needed. but again, theres only one shot over the whole movies that popped up a question in my mind, i take that as a win.

very good. genuinely did not expect it to be this good.

films.title: Four Seasons in Java
films.descriptionHtml:
Walked in expecting a revenge film—i mean all the ingredients are there. But the revenge never comes, not really. which is why when it ends, this feels like a sad film wearing revenge clothes. Theres so much sadness and anger here.

The film wants to be two things at once. A thrilling women rage, and a magical realism about female sadness. There's UFOs, ghosts, creatures, a dead man whose entire body is white light. And for inspirational concern we do know where it comes from, i get why the need of using magical realism here; reality portrayed is so comical it hurts and sad to keep filming it straight. But my view of it more like the two tracks of what the film wanted to be seemingly never merge, because the body of the story wants to keep telling a straight narrative, while the formal aspect want to play with the mythical dreamy logic. Almost the same problem i found with Edwin's Sleep No More, albeit more toned down.

Then for me it just felt like two films running side by side, not really a nuisance for me here frankly. That maybe makes directorial intent look honest at least, or just a little too much, depending where you look. but for me it seems like Kamila Andini wants to go somewhere—she knows where she wants to go—but the constraint, whatever filmmaking decision it is, audience, market, revenue etc, won't let her.

films.title: Hope
films.descriptionHtml:
When we got the news that the two titans of korean cinema were making a comeback in the same year, we were bound to eat well the whole year, and Na Hong-jin latest for me felt much more of an <i>embege</i> kind-of-disappointment. Like a rusty engine after years of disuse, there are fleeting (wrote it while listening to sarah kinsley song) glimpse of his signature brilliance; first act was solid rock! Yet the majority of the film mired in mediocrity...

The humor strains itself, 'trying to be funny' kalo kata cing abdel. Consistently fall flat, and that is not even the worst thing I could scratch my head about the movie, the characters were so caricatured never felt like i could symphatize with them. I mean??

Then there's also this utter lack of inconsistency and focus in its narrative, our protagonist framed as this anti-heroic/loser that seemingly a deliberate cynical jab approach to institutional authority. But then narrative choice keep second guessing its own characterization, suddenly at one scene he develops a rigid moral compass, after shooting his own compatriot, then later on to make some heroic actions, which turn all of this for me into exhausting experience.

And then there is the "big surprise" (you know the one). The script attempts to juggle far way too much. It wants to humanize the extraterrestrials, then back to demonize them, and then awkwardly try to make a neat resolution. This extends to their baffling stylistic choices. Why intentionally withhold subtitles for the alien dialogue for the entire film, only to spoon-feed the audience context with sudden subtitles at the very end? Why?

films.title: The Odyssey
films.descriptionHtml:
Epic, Nolan has found his formula. Which is when he using all that scale of spectacle to get inside one person, where he did that too on oppenheimer, and honestly that's is him at his best where he explored his character hyperfixation, whether its their obsession, or ego, even guilt, and ambition all at once.

Everything else is very nolan; narrative structure, image and sound, or the constant sense that something gigantic is happening. And it’s all executed so well that there’s almost nothing to argue with technically. The experience is familiar.

Still, after all this growth that he seems to had since Tenet, i couldn't find myself to find the 'perfect' nolan film, because for me there's always a lack of vulnerability that he shows a glimpse on, then pulls away from. and that’s the part i wanted more of out of his filmmaking. Can't find it here, but it's okay it doesn't have too. But perhaps in one of his next films i guess?

films.title: Disclosure Day
films.descriptionHtml:
I think there's a needful dialogue on how we treat blockbuster as pejorative on film discourse, as though scale and sincerity are somehow at odds with artistic value. If anything, the films that shaped my imagination most were the ones that embraced spectacle without embarrassment. I would not be who I am without E.T. or Jurassic Park. An affinity that explains my appreciation for this despite its obvious shortcomings.

I'd agreed with many critics that has argued that the screenplay stands as its weakest component. It does often feels disjointed. Characters drift in and out of narrative importance, thematic threads are introduced only to be partially abandoned, compromising every attempts of its own procedural ambitions. Yet, this works perfectly well in spite of those flaws. It's Spielberg operating in the register he's spent decades perfecting, those big awe-spectacle-full of sentiment and wonder. It's exactly give just a little bit of everything i need from a movie.

Perhaps that is Spielberg's special gifts—his understanding of cinema as a medium of amazement. This may not really be a good procedular thrilling movie. I can maybe find more intellectually science fiction or tight procedural thriller elsewhere. What I cannot find as easily is a filmmaker who still believes, without irony, that looking up at the unknown might change us. This one reminded me why I fell in love with movies in the first place.

films.title: Sleep No More
films.descriptionHtml:
Edwin’s most ambitious film yet, which is both a compliment and its undoing. There’s massive swing—from off-beat comedy, body horror, even cosmic dread, and social commentary—but, when you want to achieve something like this all at once, it’s usually ended up muddling the whole thing.
Formally it also hits the off-beat arthouse checklist perfectly: pulp visual, jaunty score, and dry feel-bad tragicomedy. But there’s this thing with a film with so much ambitions that what makes it less endearing despite the heights it tried to achieve, this one desperately lack irony. I think that’s the main element that makes this specific kind of surrealism work; sorry for citing another contemporary arthouse film who shared similarities, but for examples in A Useful Ghost or Chema García Ibarra’s The Sacred Spirit, an ironic detachment is used to ground the bizarre in the mundane, making the world feel lived-in. And we have very little of it here. Theres this weird pull I think between how the film wants to play around in the surreal world, and its sudden urgency to wrap things up like standard horror cinema. This culminates in a film that spends the runtime following the dynamics of the fourth of it’s character (including the factory owner), yet remains completely detached from them. I think if this either leaning much harder into those character dynamics, or just going totally off the rails into absurdity, would have done wonders. Shame tho because from what i’ve seen on screen, theres a stronger film in there somewhere.

PSA: I was completely fooled when Luthesa played the endearing character, and Rachel Amanda played the cynical one. Chuckled a bit from that. Great move. Edwin.

films.title: Ghost in the Cell
films.descriptionHtml:
At this point, ive just come to accept that walking into a Joko Anwar film means sitting through a bit of a sermon. I’ve had to tell myself to stop dare his film to explore beyond its initial premise and political cheap talks, mostly because the messaging usually ends up feeling a bit one-dimensional anyway, and no, it’s never wanted to be engaging in the first place. There are also some uncomfortable, queer-coded sexual assault jokes in this one that I’m pretty sure were thrown in for cheap comedic thrills rather than adding to the gritty reality of a prison ward (i'll wait the twitter thread to pop out later on this weekend).

But setting that misstep aside, this is honestly the most fun I’ve ever had with a Joko Anwar film. It’s highly ironic that this one delivered more laughs than actual comedies film (yes, Agak Laen 2). Kinda hilarious to leave it to a horror director to wrote some of the most entertaining and organic banter between his characters, indo comedy directors could actually take some notes.

On a final note: it’s also a bit ironic that the LSF decided to draw the censorship line at some male backside, but gave a total free pass to the fully fleshy, visceral gore in the movie. Really tell you the state of censor-hip (pun-intended) out here.

films.title: Na Willa
films.descriptionHtml: Debut Ryan sebagai sutradara live-action mengonfirmasi bahwa ia adalah seorang pentutur formalis, Na Willa dibuat bertutur dengan gambar. Gambar yang telah dipikirkan dengan matang; terasa sekali bahwa komposisi yang dipikirkan Ryan ketika merajut cerita, bukan cerita lalu memikirkan komposisi. Film dimulai dengan narasi Na Willa sebagai unreliable narrator, tapi justru karena itulah aku bisa memaklumi dan sangat menikmati semrawut magisnya dunia Na Willa. Menyenangkan dan menghangatkan hati, mungkin itu kalimat yang paling tepat. I think for all it's worth, sempat terlintas bahwa penyeragaman sifat karakter yang too good to be true, Kurangnya eksplorasi terhadap ke-wary-an Mak di awal soal keengganannya mengizinkan Willa sekolah, atau bagaimana Ryan mencoba lepas—namun tak sepenuhnya lepas—dari konteks politik karena masih menyiratkan isu rasial di sana, pada akhirnya menjadi poin-poin kritik yang tak lagi ingin kupermasalahkan. Karena Na Willa berhasil mencapai apa yang memang diimpikan oleh filmnya; merayakan sense of wonder dari kacamata seorang anak.

films.title: Sundays
films.descriptionHtml:
My god, an early contender for my favorite film of the year.

I love how it deliberately sidesteps the predictable route of critiquing religious indoctrination; it would have been so easy to use that as an attention grab for the festival circuit, yet Alauda Ruiz de Azúa refuses to fall into that trap. Instead, she explores the suffocating complexities of the family dynamics, giving us a much richer, more textual film in return.

It also helped that the soul of the film rests entirely on a magnificent performance by Blanca Soroa. Her restraint allows her to carry the weight of the entire narrative on her shoulders; every gaze and facial expression subtlely carries everything.

films.title: It Was Just an Accident
films.descriptionHtml:
After what happened to him over the past few years, it makes perfect sense that Jafar Panahi's latest work shifts his cinema into the sharp territory of the political thriller. The formal and conceptual work of the film is primarily enacted within the mobile heterotopia of Vahid's van, a space that reconfigures the semiotics of the Panahian automobile from vessel of freedom and liberty into crucible for an impossible juridical process. Panahi stages an unforgiving dialectic between physical mobility and psychic enclosure. While the vehicle travel the urban landscape, its interior remains hermetically sealed, making the exterior world almost unreachable.

This spatial logic constitutes a specific political subject-as-provisional collective forged through shared memory of trauma whose discourse-the dominant action of the film-transcodes raw impulse of vengeance into fraught, extra-legal procedure. In this regard, a metaphor of the temporality of trauma—the continuous, circular motion of a van mimes the cycle of repetition where every attempt to move forward only deepens the psychic stasis.

The Suffocating, close framing transposes the van into more than its confined space; It's an existential state, specified by the traces of violence carved into body and mind, for which there is no distance nor route of escape.

films.descriptionHtml: The momentum on this is intentionally hesitant. Zach Cregger builds scenes to an almost unbearable pitch of tension—layering atmosphere and dread—only to abruptly sever the connection at the peak of anticipation. The result is a stop-start cadence that demands a constant reset, a structural choice that borders on the maddening. And yet, this frustrating design is exactly Weapons central point. Where other films might spend its duration for convenient lore drops, Weapons instead seems intent on mirroring the characters terrifying free-fall into the unknown, thereby plunging its viewers into that same state of disorientation.

films.title: The Handmaiden
films.descriptionHtml:
Rewatched as a preparation for No Other Choice

How should we interpret Laura Mulvey's thesis on the male gaze in light of a film like The Handmaiden? Mulvey’s framework describes a world of "active/male and passive/female" looking. The Handmaiden seems to perfectly construct this world in its first half, only to meticulously dismantle it in the second by building a tender, reciprocal gaze between its two female leads.

Does this act of deliberate subversion prove the enduring relevance of Mulvey's theory, showing how filmmakers still define their work against it? Or, does the introduction of a queer, female-centric gaze—and the added layer of a colonized "mimicry" as the primary patriarchal figure—reveal the limitations of the original thesis? Does The Handmaiden suggest that to understand power in modern film, we need to look beyond Mulvey's initial focus on a male/female dynamic and also ask how colonialism and queer identity change who has the power to look?

films.title: Sore: A Wife from the Future
films.descriptionHtml:
There's a fascinating puzzle at the heart of Yandy Laurens’ Sore: Istri Dari Masa Depan, and it’s the source of the film’s unique genius. It has the soul of magical realism, bestowing its time-travel miracle with the unexplained grace of a fable. And yet, it operates with the strict, rule-based mechanics of a science-fiction plot device. It’s a magical realist soul animating a sci-fi skeleton. On paper, it absolutely should not work. It’s a paradox that should tear the story apart.

This puzzle will be irrelevant for some; they’ll be swept up in the film’s powerful emotional core, and rightfully so. But my brain couldn't let it go, not because I was searching for a flaw, but because the very thing that should have been a flaw felt, against all logic, become it's strength.

A profound film, yes, but the question that left me completely floored was one honest admiration: How the hell did he make that work?

films.title: What We Ask of a Statue is That It Doesn’t Move
Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning
films.descriptionHtml:
An absolute disaster, a stunningly stupid and infuriating end to a franchise that clearly had no idea how to wrap things up. The decision to shoot this thing without a finished script wasn't some bold artistic choice; it was a catastrophic blunder that resulted in an incoherent mess. We were promised a grand finale against a world-ending AI, but what we got was a series of increasingly ridiculous stunts strung together by a flimsy plot.

The biggest joke is the "Entity" itself, this supposedly all-powerful AI. It's built up as this terrifying digital god that can end the world, but then it just... sits there. For huge chunks of the movie, this omniscient AI basically lets Ethan Hunt and his crew collect all the plot coupons they need: the core module, the sub coordinates, the mighty "Poison Pill"—with barely a peep. Its main human agent, Gabriel, is more focused on being a narcissistic, out-of-touch villain who doesn't even seem to know what he wants. A world-ending AI wouldn't play these silly games; it would just end things. The movie hints at big ideas about AI and global power, then immediately forgets them to show Tom Cruise doing impossible things (which, unironically, are often the best parts of these movies). The villain is a complete pushover, making the entire central conflict feel pointless and stupid.

Watching Ethan Hunt perform his magic can be viscerally entertaining. But here’s the rub: when you know this is supposed to be his grand farewell, the stakes feel utterly manufactured and emotionally hollow. We know he's going to survive every ludicrous predicament because the franchise has conditioned us to it, and a farewell without actual, palpable risk is no farewell at all. His plot armor is thicker than ever, which is precisely the opposite of what you need when trying to generate emotional investment in a character's final outing. Compare this to Daniel Craig's James Bond in No Time To Die. That film, for all its own narrative choices, understood that a true farewell requires sacrifice, consequence, and a sense of irrevocable finality. Bond’s ending, whether you loved it or hated it, cost him something profound, giving his departure weight and emotional resonance. Ethan, by contrast, just seems to be going through another extreme Tuesday, which is infuriating when we're meant to believe this is the end of an era.

films.title: The Siege at Thorn High
films.descriptionHtml:
Rasanya seperti bayang-bayang kutipan Adorno menghantuiku setelah menonton film ini. Kalimatnya yang terkenal "Menulis puisi setelah Auschwitz adalah tindakan barbar" terus terngiang, menghadirkan pertanyaan-pertanyaan sulit setiap kali menonton dan membaca karya seni yang mencoba menyentuh wilayah trauma sejarah yang begitu dalam. Pergulatanku dengan kutipan itu bukan karena aku percaya bahwa seni menjadi hal mustahil atau terlarang setelah tragedi. Justru sebaliknya, seni mungkin menjadi respons naluriah manusia yang paling perlu untuk melawan dan mengingat. Bagiku yang paling menusuk dari peringatan Adorno bukan soal boleh atau tidaknya, melainkan soal bagaimana. Tentang bahaya ketika seni, dalam upayanya untuk mewakili penderitaan, justru secara tidak sadar komplisit (bukan berarti film ini komplisit), menjadikannya bisa dikonsumsi dengan cara yang mengkhianati realitasnya.

Dan justru risiko itulah yang terasa mengendap dalam film ini, terutama dalam cara ia memaknai kerusuhan Jakarta 1998. Meskipun disajikan sebagai fiksi futuristik, benang-benang narasinya tidak dapat dipungkiri diambil dari sejarah yang nyata. Ini bukan fantasi semata, film ini dengan gamblang mengalirkan kembali peristiwa Mei '98. Tapi keterlibatan kritis dengan sejarah seperti ini menuntut kesadaran bahwa “fakta” sejarah, terutama yang menyangkut kekejaman massal, tidak pernah netral. Fakta selalu ditafsirkan, dibingkai, dan dalam kasus ini coba diadaptasi melalui narasi visual yang meminjam bentuk fiksi untuk mencoba menyentil kebenaran yang lebih dalam.

Di sinilah filmnya diuji secara kritis. Film ini memang efektif secara emosional, ketakutan yang dibangun terasa nyata, ketegangannya menghantam, dan simpati terhadap karakter Edwin muncul seketika. Tapi saat menyaksikan kekerasan di dalam sekolah yang terasa begitu tertata, bahkan nyaris seperti koreografi yang mengerikan, sulit mengabaikan rasa bahwa ada sesuatu yang esensial yang terpinggirkan. Kengerian yang hadir, sekuat apapun dampaknya, seperti diberi panggung utama, sementara aspek-aspek yang lebih sunyi dan mendalam untuk menggali "mengapa" kebencian dan kengerian itu eksis justru terpinggirkan.

Ketika menyaksikan latar kota (presumably) Jakarta di masa depan dalam film ini, aku memiliki perasaan akan adanya sesuatu yang hilang dalam dunia yang dibangun oleh Joko disini. Memang, Joko secara eksplisit menampilkan ketimpangan ekonomi, perpecahan rasial, dan ketegangan horizontal di bagian awal. Namun, jika masa depan yang digambarkan dimaksudkan sebagai alegori atas kondisi tahun 1998, masih belum terlihat representasi yang meyakinkan tentang arsitektur sistemik yang secara logis dapat menjelaskan munculnya kekerasan yang terstruktur dan berpola seperti itu. Karena kekerasan Mei '98 bukanlah ledakan spontan, ia memiliki preseden yang jelas. Dibangun di atas kebijakan diskriminatif selama puluhan tahun, manipulasi ekonomi sebagai senjata politik, dan keterlibatan negara yang terdokumentasi.

Tanpa kejelasan struktur tersebut, kekerasan fiksional yang digambarkan dalam bukit duri terasa lepas dari akar sejarah dan menjadi kekacauan generik yang bisa terjadi di mana saja dan kapan saja. Bayang-bayang panjang dari kebijakan diskriminatif, manipulasi negara yang penuh perhitungan, serta keputusasaan ekonomi yang dijadikan senjata hanya hadir sebagai bisikan latar, nyaris tenggelam oleh dentuman ancaman monster dalam manifestasi anak sekolah dan detak waktu yang mencekam. Alih-alih mencoba mengulik akar penyakitnya, Bukit Duri tampak lebih memilih untuk menampilkan gejalanya dengan spektakel, mengabaikan sistem yang melahirkannya.

films.descriptionHtml:
The film’s cardinal sin lies in its compulsive need to layer suspense upon suspense, a strategy that initially intrigues but quickly turn into shortsighted choice. Without anchoring these moments to characters whose fates invoke empathy, the tension dissipates into abstraction. The script’s refusal to linger on emotional beats reduces its protagonists to pawns in a labyrinthine game with no stakes that the audience cares to witness resolved. A pivotal subplot involving a troubled past is introduced in fragmented flashbacks, but these are treated as perfunctory nods to “depth” rather than genuine explorations of motive or trauma.

Compounding this issue is the film’s disjointed rhythm. Transitions often feel abrupt, abandoning one thread of suspense to chase another without narrative payoff. If Dark Nuns avoids collapsing entirely into incoherence, it is solely due to Song Hye-Kyo’s commanding presence.

Compounding this issue is the film’s disjointed rhythm. Transitions often feel abrupt, abandoning one thread of suspense to chase another without narrative payoff. If Dark Nuns avoids collapsing entirely into incoherence, it is solely due to Song Hye-Kyo’s commanding presence.

films.title: All We Imagine as Light
films.descriptionHtml:
The film resonates with me due to its capacity to encompass both struggle and hope. Prabha invests her emotions into her profession, despite her personal life seeming stagnant. Also, in the manner that Anu boldly embraces love, despite the perception that the world may oppose her. Parvaty persistently advocates for her home on the city, despite how the city has its own efforts to progress without her.

And there is a sort of shared optimism in the voids between these lives, whether it's in the glances they exchange, in the silent times when their hardships cross. Not the type that assures everything will be OK, but the type that encourages perseverance. It’s in the way they show up for each other, in the small acts of kindness and resilience that fill through their days.

films.title: Caught by the Tides
films.descriptionHtml:
In many ways, this feels like Jia at his most vulnerable and introspective. In contrast to his earlier works like Still Life and A Touch of Sin, which directly addressed the violence of progress, he now appears more focused on exploring the subtle devastation it results in. What emerges is arguably his most intimate film to date - a nuanced yet resolute examination of how humans bear their past, while the surroundings become unrecognizable.

I couldn't get rid of the impression that I had not just seen an epilogue of his career, but also a profound meditation on memory, progress, and the cost of forgetting. Jia has crafted something uniquely tied to China’s story yet universally relatable, capturing moments caught between tides of change.

films.title: Monisme
films.descriptionHtml: I liked the post-colonial approach in Monisme, remind me much of Weerasethakul's Memoria (2021). What struck me most was how Rizaldi uses the figure of the mystic as a counter-narrative to the modern, scientific, rational Western worldview. The mystic’s connection to Merapi is not one of fear or domination, but one of unity and reverence. Rizaldi doesn’t present this indigenous worldview in opposition to the scientist’s rationalism in a simplistic, binary way. Instead, both perspectives coexist within the film’s polyphonic structure, each presenting a legitimate form of knowledge, without privileging one over the other.

films.title: Kinds of Kindness
films.descriptionHtml:
While this may not be Yorgos Lanthimos' best film, it does represent the pinnacle of his auteurist concerns. Control, the macabre, and the precariousness of individual agency within institutional and interpersonal contexts are the central preoccupations that have defined his body of work, and these themes are all well captured here.

Society, institutional authorities, and personal relationships all work together to deprive individuals of their autonomy, and this is something that has always captivated Lanthimos. His films have always revolved around this central theme of control, whether it's the inflexible social norms in Dogtooth (2009) or the ludicrous power struggles in The Killing of a Sacred Deer (2017). The tripartite narrative structure of Kinds of Kindness brings this issue to a head by examining economic, psychological, and physical aspects of control. This allows for a more all-encompassing look at how freedom of choice is illusion in Lanthimos's world. (4/5)

films.title: The Beast
films.descriptionHtml:
Struktur narasi yang tidak beraturan dari The Beasts sangat mencolok dan mencerminkan gagasan postmodern tentang identitas sebagai sesuatu yang dinamis dan tidak lengkap. Manusia bukanlah entitas yang tetap, tetapi dibentuk oleh berbagai peristiwa, yang masing-masing menarik mereka ke arah yang berbeda. Tidak seperti film kebanyakan yang memiliki alur cerita tentang penemuan jati diri, The Beasts menggantinya dengan narasi postmodern tentang dislokasi dan disintegrasi. Perjalanan Gabrielle bukanlah perjalanan menuju pencerahan atau purifikasi perasaan, melainkan perjalanan menuju kebingungan dan alienasi. Struktur film yang terfragmentasi mencerminkan disorientasi psikologis ini, karena Gabrielle dipaksa untuk menghadapi kenyataan bahwa identitasnya tidak dapat dimurnikan. Seperti semua subjek postmodern, film ini merupakan kumpulan fragmen dan kontradiksi.

'Beast' yang sebenarnya dalam The Beasts bukanlah bencana eksternal, melainkan kesadaran batin bahwa keterpisahan emosional, kontrol teknologi, dan penolakan terhadap hubungan antarmanusia hanya akan membawa pada rasa terisolasi dan kehilangan yang lebih dalam. (5/5)

films.title: The Substance
films.descriptionHtml:
The Substance tampaknya begitu terperangkap dalam representasi ekstrim dan efek-efek mengerikan yang coba dipertontonkannya, sehingga ia seolah-olah "memaksa" kita untuk menelan adegan-adegan menjijikkan ini. Pertanyaannya, apa yang ingin dicapai dengan ini? Visual yang mengerikan memang tak terbantahkan, tetapi pada akhirnya, efek berulang dari ketidaknyamanan yang ditimbulkannya hanya berujung pada pertanyaan tentang signifikansi dari pendekatan ini. Karakter-karakternya mengalami transformasi grotesk dalam bentuk body horror yang berlebihan dan membingungkan.

Ada upaya tersirat untuk memberikan kritik terhadap bagaimana tubuh dikomodifikasi, namun ironi muncul ketika film ini sendiri terjebak dalam jebakan yang sama—mengubah tubuh karakter menjadi objek tontonan yang eksploitatif demi kejutan visual. Di sini, pesan kritis yang mungkin ingin ditelaah justru kabur di balik lapisan-lapisan absurditas, dan akhirnya film ini berakhir sebagai bentuk hiburan visual tanpa 'substansi' yang berarti, meskipun berniat menentang hal tersebut. (2/5)

lists.title: 2024 End Year List: Documentary
lists.descriptionHtml:
This year, I decided to separate fiction and documentary films in my end-of-year list. So much has happened in the world, and just ranking them as personal favorites felt wrong—it seemed to downplay the urgency of the issues we’re facing.

  • No Other Land

    There is no other documentary you need to watch more than this one. Against the backdrop of the ongoing Gaza genocide, No Other Land offers a searing portrayal of perpetual colonialism and the brutal realities faced by Palestinian villagers in Masafer Yatta. The film’s raw, unflinching narrative exposes the structural violence and relentless demolitions inflicted upon these communities while celebrating their unyielding spirit of resistance.

  • Soundtrack to a Coup d'Etat

    Through archival footage and an chaoting editing, Grimonprez navigates this complex episode of the start of Pax Americana order. His approach to storytelling mirrors the improvisational nature of jazz, where rhythms of tension and release echo the political upheavals of the time. Despite the intensity and fragmented nature of the visuals, Grimonprez ensures that the documentary never loses sight of its central message. The chaotic flow of images, sounds, and voices comes together in a way that distills the heart of this historical moment, making it comprehensible even to those unfamiliar with cold-war international politics.

  • Monisme

    I liked the post-colonial approach in Monisme, remind me much of Weerasethakul's Memoria (2021). What struck me most was how Rizaldi uses the figure of the mystic as a counter-narrative to the modern, scientific, rational Western worldview. Rizaldi doesn’t present this indigenous worldview in opposition to the scientist’s rationalism in a simplistic, binary way. Instead, both perspectives coexist within the film’s polyphonic structure, each presenting a legitimate form of knowledge, without privileging one over the other.

  • Dahomey

    As I wrote this excerpt, i realize the movies on my list are underlined an ongoing relevance of the post-colonial movement and its exploration of the lasting effects of colonialism. Each film, in its unique way, speaks to the complexities of power, identity, and on this, restitution,

    On Dahomey, Mati Diop brings a poetic sensibility to this weighty topic, elevating the narrative beyond legal or political debates into something far more human and profound. The objects being returned represent the stories, identities, and legacies of a people who were once colonized and stripped of their history.

  • The Gullspång Miracle

    Encapsulating the notion that life is stranger than fiction, it employs layered narratives that juggle the complexities of identity construction. Each twist and piece of information could becomes its own intriguing story. Maria Fredriksson’s direction has this uncanny ability to pull you into the mystery, and by the end, I couldn’t stop thinking about how fragile our understanding of “truth” really is. This is the kind of documentary that lingers in my mind long after the credits roll.

    Human stories, as this illustrates, can be both fascinating and terrifying.

  • Afternoons of Solitude

  • Ryuichi Sakamoto | Opus
  • The Night Won't End
  • Trains
